cues.text: A Boy King Raised by a Formidable Mother
Born at Poissy in 1214 (or 1215, by some reckonings), Louis became King of France at only eleven or twelve years old when his father, Louis VIII, died.
His mother, Blanche of Castile , ruled as regent through his minority, instilling in him a Christian formation of exceptional intensity and seriousness.
By his own later account, she famously told him that she would rather see him dead than guilty of committing a single mortal sin.
Blanche governed the kingdom with real political skill through years of baronial rebellion and foreign threat.
She defeated a coalition led by the Count de la Marche in league with King Henry III of England, securing the throne for her son.

By the time he assumed full personal rule at twenty-one, this formation had prepared him for a reign that would combine genuine political competence with a depth of personal piety unusual even for a medieval Christian monarch.
A King Known for Personal Justice
As sole ruler, Louis earned a widespread reputation for personal fairness and accessibility, unusual among medieval monarchs.
He was remembered for literally sitting beneath an oak tree in the forest of Vincennes, hearing ordinary subjects’ grievances and rendering judgment in person.
He did so without the formal barriers of court procedure that typically separated a king from his people.
This reputation for justice extended well beyond his own kingdom's borders.
Foreign rulers, including the English King Henry III, sought Louis out as an impartial arbitrator for their own disputes—a mark of trust rarely extended to a reigning monarch by his political rivals.
Crusade as a Vow, Not a Conquest
Struck down by a severe illness in 1244, Louis vowed, upon his recovery, to take up the cross and lead a crusade to the Holy Land.
This vow was undertaken not out of political ambition but as a genuine act of religious devotion.
He departed on his first crusade in 1248, spending years in the Holy Land and Egypt.
The campaign ended in military disaster, Louis's own capture, and ransom.
He remained in the Holy Land for several more years afterward, strengthening the fortifications and position of the remaining Christian territories before finally returning to France in 1254.
A Second Crusade, and a Death Near Tunis
Despite the failure of his first crusade, Louis's religious devotion drove him to undertake a second in 1270, this time directed toward Tunis in North Africa.
The campaign was struck almost immediately by an outbreak of disease among the crusading army.
Louis himself fell gravely ill and died near Tunis on 25 August 1270, having achieved little of his crusade's original strategic aims.
Yet he remained, to his final hour, faithful to the religious vow that had first sent him east a quarter-century earlier.
A Patron of Learning and the Arts
Beyond his military campaigns, Louis's reign left a lasting cultural legacy: he founded the Sorbonne in Paris, one of medieval Europe's great centers of learning.

He also commissioned the exquisite Sainte-Chapelle in Paris to house relics of Christ's Passion he had acquired at great expense—a building still regarded as one of the supreme achievements of Gothic architecture.
Legacy
Louis was canonized in 1297, less than three decades after his death, and remains, to this day, the only King of France ever recognized as a saint by the Catholic Church.

Remembered not primarily for military success — both his crusades ended in failure — but for sustained personal holiness, Louis IX expressed justice, humility, and genuine devotion at the very center of worldly power.
He stands as the enduring medieval model of the Christian ruler: a king who never forgot that the crown he wore was, in the end, held in trust from a King greater than himself.
